lines.text: If your Meta ads are reaching everyone, they're converting no one. Here's exactly why.

Broad targeting means you're paying to show your ad to people who will never hire you. A plumber reaching every adult in the city is paying for renters, apartment dwellers, people who handle everything themselves. You're not buying leads — you're buying noise. Meta's algorithm needs a specific signal to find the right person. Give it a wide net and it guesses.

The fix is specificity. Who actually hires you — homeowners, certain suburbs, specific demographics, people who've already shown interest in home services. Narrow that down and Meta starts finding people who look like your actual customers. Cost per lead drops. Lead quality goes up. The same budget does more work.
Less reach, better leads. That trade is always worth making.

scripts.title: The 3-Second Hook Formula (Why Most Ads Die Immediately)
scripts.film: Screen record the Miro board at https://miro.com/app/board/BOARD_3_ID=/. Walk through each section top to bottom — pause cursor on each box, read the key point, then move on. Calm and methodical. The board is doing the visual teaching. Your voice is the commentary.

captions.text: most ads die in the first 3 seconds — not because the offer is bad, but because the hook doesn't stop anyone. the formula is simple: pattern interrupt, one piece of real value, one clear action. most businesses aren't doing any of them right.

captions.label: C
captions.text: 3 seconds to earn the next 27.

lines.text: Your ad has three seconds before someone scrolls past it forever. Here's the exact formula for making those three seconds count.

Seconds one to three — the pattern interrupt. You need to say or show something that makes their thumb stop. Not your logo. Not your company name. Something that speaks directly to a problem they're already living. A plumber who opens with 'water bill gone up lately?' stops more scrolls than 'ABC Plumbing, serving your area.' Start with them. Not you.

Seconds four to twenty — one clear piece of value. Not three tips. Not a full service rundown. One insight that makes them think: I didn't know that, or — that's exactly my problem. The moment someone learns something from your ad, you become the authority. That's when trust begins and they keep watching.

Last ten seconds — one clear next step. Not 'visit the website' and 'give us a call' and 'follow for more tips.' One action. The more options you give them, the less likely they are to do any of them. Pick the one you want and make it as easy as possible to take.
Interrupt. Deliver value. Direct to one action. That's it.

lines.text: If you're spending your entire budget on cold traffic and barely running retargeting — you're doing it backwards.

Look at this cold traffic campaign. New people, never heard of the business. Cost per lead is decent but you're working hard to get there. Meta has to show the ad multiple times before anyone converts because there's zero prior trust. These people don't know your work, haven't seen your results, have no reason to choose you over anyone else.

Now look at the retargeting campaign. Same business, same offer. But these are people who visited the website, saw a post, maybe even filled in a form and didn't book. They're warm. The trust is already there. You're not convincing anyone — you're just showing up again at the right moment and reminding them why they were interested in the first place.

Cost per lead from retargeting is almost always lower. You're paying to close, not to introduce. And the quality is higher because these people already chose to engage with your business. That's where your ad budget works the hardest — and most service businesses completely ignore it.
Cold traffic builds the funnel. Retargeting converts it. Run both.

scripts.title: One word that kills your ad performance
scripts.film: Film in natural light, close-up shot from chest up. Direct eye contact with camera. Casual setting like your office or workspace. Lean in slightly when you reveal the word — make it feel like you're sharing something that actually matters.

captions.label: A
captions.text: most ads use weak words. swap this one and watch click rates jump.

captions.text: the word "get" kills your ads. one swap doubles your clicks. here's what to use instead and why it works.

captions.text: change one word in your ad copy and your click rate goes up. period.

lines.text: I see the same word in almost every service business ad, and it's costing you clicks. Let me tell you what it is and what to swap it for.
The word is 'get.' Get a free quote. Get your gutters cleaned. Get a consultation. It's everywhere, and honestly, it's lazy. It doesn't create any urgency or benefit in the person's mind.

Instead, use action words that speak to the actual outcome they want. 'Schedule your free inspection.' 'Book your plumbing fix today.' 'Protect your home from water damage.' See the difference? One shows them what happens. The other just says... get something.
When you test this swap on your ads, you're not just changing words — you're changing how people feel about clicking. They see benefit. They see movement. They click more often.
Next time you're writing ad copy, catch yourself saying 'get' and replace it with something that shows the actual value. Your click rate will thank you.

lines.text: everyone tells me I should run Google ads for my plumbing business. I don't. here's why.

Google is intent-based. Someone types 'plumber near me' and you're fighting everyone else who's already bidding on that exact keyword. you win the bid, you get the click, but so does everyone else paying the same amount.

Meta is reach-based. You're showing up in feeds of people in your service area—people who aren't even thinking about needing you yet. But when their pipe bursts at midnight, guess who they remember? The ad they saw last week.

For service businesses specifically, reach and frequency beat expensive high-intent clicks. You want to own the neighborhood before the problem happens. Meta lets you do that at a fraction of what Google costs.
That's the whole game for local service work. Be everywhere they are, before they need you.

scripts.title: How Meta's Algorithm Picks Who Sees Your Ad
scripts.film: Screen record in Meta Ads Manager. Start on the campaign level, then drill into the audience section and targeting settings. Click through to show the relevance score, estimated reach, and learning phase indicator. Keep mouse movements smooth and deliberate. Speak naturally over the screens—no need to rush. Use a plumber or HVAC example in your head to keep it concrete.

captions.label: A
captions.text: meta doesn't just show your ad to everyone in your targeting—it learns who actually converts and prioritizes them

captions.label: B
captions.text: your first 50 conversions are the most important. that's when meta's algorithm learns who your real customer is. after that it gets way smarter about who sees it.

captions.label: C
captions.text: meta optimizes for conversions, not clicks. it will ignore your targeting if it finds a better audience.

lines.text: Your targeting doesn't matter as much as you think. Here's why.
When you set up an ad, you pick an audience—maybe homeowners aged 35 to 65 in your service area. But Meta doesn't just show your ad to everyone in that box. It starts broad and then learns.

Every time someone in your audience sees your ad and converts—that's a lead, a call, a booked job—Meta records that. And it uses that data to find more people just like them. It literally rewires who sees your ad based on real results.

That's why those first 50 conversions are gold. That's Meta's training period. Once it has enough data, it stops guessing and starts finding your actual customer. Your targeting becomes way less important than your conversion data.
Tight targeting matters early. But the algorithm will always override it if it finds a better customer. That's how you win with ads.
